issues.subcategory: Sample description contradiction (student vs. national probability)
issues.description: The abstract, introduction, and discussion repeatedly describe the data as a 'national probability sample' / 'nationally representative sample' of the general population. However, the Methods section states participants were recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington,' with a mean age of 19 and an intro-psych pool source. These are mutually exclusive descriptions. This is not a trivial inconsistency: the paper's entire interpretive framework rests on the claim that its results differ from prior student-sample findings (Stanley et al. [14]) precisely because it uses a general-population sample. If the sample is actually students, the central explanatory argument collapses.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1

issues.subcategory: Measure does not match the named construct
issues.description: The outcome variable is labeled 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' / 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment' (WILL) throughout the title, abstract, analysis, and results. However, the Measures section operationalizes it as environmental *concern*, using items 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?' Concern is an attitudinal/affective construct, not behavioral willingness or sacrifice. Every behavioral and causal interpretation about 'making personal sacrifices' is therefore built on a measure that does not assess that construct.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.subcategory: Representativeness overclaim
issues.description: The authors claim their results are 'highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population' on the basis of a 'nationally representative sample.' Given the Methods describe a single-university introductory-psychology pool (mean age 19, 68% female, 86% Pākehā), the sample is neither nationally representative nor probability-based, and the generalizability claim is unsupported. Even the demographic composition (overwhelmingly young, female, NZ-European students) deviates substantially from the NZ population.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from correlational/cross-lagged data
issues.description: The authors repeatedly assert causal conclusions ('there is a causal pathway,' 'SDO having a causal effect,' 'the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism') from a cross-lagged panel design. Cross-lagged correlational designs cannot establish causation; they are vulnerable to unmeasured confounding (which the authors themselves acknowledge as a 'third variable' possibility), and temporal precedence alone does not license causal claims. The strength of these causal statements is inconsistent with the design and with the authors' own caveats about third variables.
issues.quote: With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.subcategory: Standard error mislabeled as standard deviation
issues.description: Reported parameter uncertainty is labeled 'SD' (standard deviation) throughout the results (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'). For a path coefficient, the reported value should be the standard error (SE) of the estimate, not a standard deviation. The very small values (.01, .002, .003) confirm these are standard errors. Mislabeling is confusing and affects interpretation/replicability.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.subcategory: Selective interpretation of model fit indices
issues.description: The model shows a very large and significant chi-square and a CFI of .86, which is below conventional thresholds (~.90/.95) and indicates poor fit. The authors discount this by attributing it to 'model complexity' and accept the model based only on the fit indices that look favorable (RMSEA, SRMR). This selective reasoning about fit, without reporting alternative model comparisons or justification for the complexity claim, is a researcher-degrees-of-freedom concern. CFI is not primarily a 'complexity-affected' index, so the rationale is questionable.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion and unreported attrition across five waves
issues.description: The analysis used listwise deletion across five measurement waves, which can substantially bias estimates and reduce power if dropout is non-random; modern approaches (FIML, multiple imputation) are standard for longitudinal SEM. The manuscript provides no information on how many participants began the study, the retention/attrition rate, attrition patterns, or whether dropout was related to study variables, deferring all of this to an external website. This prevents evaluation of bias and replicability.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.subcategory: Improper comparison of dependent correlations via CI overlap
issues.description: The authors conclude that the SDO–environmentalism correlation is significantly stronger than the RWA–environmentalism correlation based on non-overlapping confidence intervals. These two correlations are dependent (both share the environmentalism variable), so a proper test (e.g., Steiger's test for dependent correlations) is required. Non-overlap of marginal CIs is neither necessary nor sufficient for a significant difference, especially for dependent correlations.
issues.quote: the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.subcategory: Low reliability of short scales
issues.description: The reliabilities for the key predictors are low (SDO = .69, RWA = .70) and the outcome is a 2-item measure (.76). The authors acknowledge the low reliabilities but proceed without correction or discussion of attenuation. Low reliability attenuates observed relationships and undermines comparisons of predictive strength between SDO and RWA, which is the paper's central inferential claim.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.subcategory: Measurement non-invariance from a dropped item
issues.description: One RWA item was not administered at Time 2 but was included at all other waves. The authors then impose a 'stationary' model constraining residual variances for the same item to be equal across time. A missing indicator at one wave undermines the assumption of strict longitudinal measurement invariance underlying the time-invariant constraints, yet no test of measurement invariance is reported and the handling of the missing item in the constrained model is not described.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory significance threshold
issues.description: The Data Analysis section states a significance threshold of p < .05, while the Figure 1 caption states paths meet a threshold of p < .01 unless otherwise noted. These conflicting alpha levels create ambiguity about which criterion was applied to which results and how 'significance' was determined.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: Redundant/contradictory description of model constraints
issues.description: The description of constraints repeats the same statement twice ('We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations... to be the same in each measurement point' and 'Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point'), which is internally redundant and obscures exactly which constraints were imposed in what order, hindering replication.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points. Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration or justification for stationarity decision
issues.description: Numerous analytic choices (imposing stationarity/time-invariant constraints, equating residual variances, model acceptance criteria, choice of indicators) are made without pre-registration or sensitivity analyses. The decision to constrain effects to be time-invariant is justified only by interest, not tested against a freely-estimated alternative, leaving researcher degrees of freedom undisclosed.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of distinct paradigm constructs (DSP vs. NEP)
issues.description: The authors attribute the 'dominant social paradigm (DSP)' to Noe and Snow [15], but that reference concerns the 'new environmental paradigm (NEP)' scale ('The new environmental paradigm and further scale analysis'). The DSP and NEP are distinct (indeed opposing) constructs, so attributing the DSP to a NEP-scale source reflects a conceptual/citation mismatch that misrepresents the theoretical basis being invoked.
issues.quote: This idea of human dominance over nature is evident in anthropocentric depictions of our relationship with the natural environment, a belief that is at the core of Noe and Snow’s [15] dominant social paradigm (DSP).

issues.subcategory: Unspecified measurement intervals
issues.description: The study is described as spanning 'five years' across 'five semesters' (2009–2013), but the actual time lags between the five waves are never specified. Cross-lagged effect sizes depend on the interval between waves; without specifying the lags (and whether they were equal), the time-invariance assumption cannot be evaluated and the study cannot be replicated or properly interpreted.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.subcategory: Mplus version inconsistency
issues.description: The text states analyses were conducted in Mplus version 7.3, but the cited user's guide reference [29] is the Sixth Edition (1998–2010), corresponding to Mplus version 6. This minor inconsistency may reflect imprecise reporting of the software actually used.
issues.quote: was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29])

issues.subcategory: Strong directional/socialization inference from a single coefficient
issues.description: From the finding that RWA predicts SDO over time but not vice versa, the authors draw a broad cultural-causal conclusion that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This is a substantial overinterpretation of an asymmetric cross-lagged coefficient, ignoring measurement reliability differences, variance differences, and alternative explanations for cross-lag asymmetries.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.subcategory: Garbled/missing test statistic notation
issues.description: Chi-square difference tests are reported without the chi-square symbol (e.g., '2(1) = 2.34, p = .126'; '2(1) = 39.97'; '2(1) = 15,389.13'), making it ambiguous what statistic is reported. While likely a formatting artifact, the omission impairs clarity and verification of the reported model-comparison tests.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor

issues.subcategory: Inference of 'no difference' from a non-significant model comparison
issues.description: The authors claim SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA, yet their own constrained-vs-unconstrained model comparison (Δχ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126) fails to reject the hypothesis that the two paths are equal. They nonetheless interpret SDO as stronger 'based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients.' This is a logical inconsistency: the formal test does not support a difference, so the central conclusion of differential predictive strength is not statistically justified.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.subcategory: Two-item outcome combining heterogeneous content
issues.description: The environmentalism outcome combines a 'concern about the natural environment' item with a 'environmental problems have been exaggerated' (denial-type) item into a single two-item index. These tap somewhat different constructs (affective concern vs. skepticism/denial), and a two-indicator latent or composite provides weak coverage of the broad 'environmentalism' construct being theorized, limiting construct validity and the breadth of conclusions.
issues.quote: Participants responded on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much), with a midpoint of 4 (somewhat).
